en.note: The English alphabet. Each letter has a short word to hold it.

items.name: x
items.gloss: a box; x is inside the word

de.note: German has ä, ö, ü, and ß after the shared letters.

nl.note: Dutch uses the Latin alphabet. IJ is one sound, taught with the letters.

da.note: Danish ends with æ, ø, and å. They are separate letters.

gsw.note: Zürich German spelling. Swiss writing uses ss, not ß.

es.note: Spanish adds ñ. The accent marks the stressed syllable.

fr.note: French uses the Latin alphabet. Accents and ç change the vowel or the c.

pt.note: Brazilian Portuguese. Ç and the tildes belong to the spelling.

it.note: Italian. H is silent, and it keeps c and g hard.

ro.note: Romanian adds ă, â, î, ș, and ț.

eo.note: Esperanto adds ĉ, ĝ, ĥ, ĵ, ŝ, and ŭ. The ending tells you the job of the word.

tr.note: Turkish has no q, w, or x. Dotless ı and dotted i are different letters.

sq.note: Albanian treats dh, gj, ll, nj, rr, sh, th, xh, and zh as single letters.

hr.note: Croatian writes č, ć, dž, đ, lj, nj, š, and ž as letters of the alphabet.

sl.note: Slovenian adds č, š, and ž.

pl.note: Polish keeps ą, ę, ł, and the accented consonants. A few never start a word.

cs.note: Czech includes á, č, ď, é, ě, í, ň, ó, ř, š, ť, ú, ů, ý, ž, and the letter ch.

sk.note: Slovak is close to Czech, with ä, ô, ľ, ĺ, ŕ, dz, and dž.

ru.note: Russian has 33 letters. ъ, ы, and ь rarely start a word.

uk.note: Ukrainian uses і, ї, є, and ґ. The letter и is a different vowel from і.

bg.note: Bulgarian has no cases on the noun, but the alphabet still has ъ and ь.

mk.note: Macedonian uses ѓ, ќ, ѕ, љ, њ, and џ.

sr.note: The course writes Serbian in Cyrillic. The same alphabet is also written in Latin.

el.note: Greek has 24 letters. The accent shows the stressed vowel.

hy.note: Eastern Armenian. Learn the letter with a short word.

items.name: վյուն
items.gloss: coffee; ւ is the second part of ու

he.note: Hebrew reads right to left. Vowels are marked here so the word can be read aloud.

ar.note: Modern Standard, Egyptian, and Saudi share these letters. The memory word changes with the variety.

fa.note: Persian adds پ, چ, ژ, and گ to the Arabic letters.

ur.note: Urdu reads right to left. It adds ٹ, ڈ, ڑ, and a few marks to the Arabic base.

arc.note: Classical Syriac. The letter keeps its old name, and the word is one you already meet in the course when it can.

ber.note: Standard Moroccan Tamazight in Tifinagh. The reading is the Latin spelling.

ko.note: Hangul letters combine into a syllable block. Learn the pieces, then the block.

th.note: Thai consonants are remembered by their traditional names. Class matters for the tone.

vi.note: Vietnamese letters include ă, â, ê, ô, ơ, ư, and đ. Tone marks sit on the vowel.

id.note: Indonesian spelling is close to the sound. There is no grammatical gender.

tl.note: Modern Filipino uses the Latin alphabet, including the older ng.

mg.note: Malagasy uses the Latin alphabet. The word you want often comes first in the sentence.

sw.note: Swahili uses Latin letters. Ch, sh, ny, and ng' are single sounds.

so.note: Somali spelling matches the sound. C, x, and q are throat sounds.

ha.note: Hausa in Boko, the Latin school spelling. Ɓ, ɗ, and ƙ change the sound.

yo.note: Yoruba tones and the underdots are part of the spelling. Keep them.

ig.note: Igbo underdots and the digraphs gb, gh, kp, and nw are letters, not decorations.

ln.note: Kinshasa Lingala. Accents mark the tone. Ɛ and ɔ are vowels of their own.

ff.note: Fulfulde in Latin letters. Ɓ, ɗ, and ƴ are not the same as b, d, and y.

qu.note: Southern Quechua, in the spelling used on the cards. Apostrophes mark a sharp consonant.

gn.note: Paraguayan Guaraní. The tilde and the nasal vowels belong to the word.

hi.note: Hindi vowels and consonants. The inherent a is part of the consonant until a vowel mark replaces it.

mr.note: Marathi uses Devanagari and adds ळ. The verb agrees with the subject.

bn.note: Bengali has no grammatical gender. The vowel marks sit on the consonant.

gu.note: Gujarati vowels and consonants. The verb agrees with gender and number.

ta.note: Tamil vowels and consonants. A few consonants rarely start a word, so the example holds them inside it.

te.note: Telugu vowels and consonants. Long and short vowels are different letters.

ml.note: Malayalam vowels and consonants. The reading shows the long vowels.

zh.note: Every character that appears on a Chinese card in this course. The stroke order plays on the right. One-character words come first.
